Here is a detailed persuasive essay in that spirit:

Why the United States Should Embrace Sortition in Government

American democracy is in a period of deep frustration. Elections are supposed to give citizens power, but many people feel that the system no longer responds to ordinary voters. Campaigns are dominated by fundraising, political parties drive people into opposing camps, and elected officials often spend more time positioning for reelection than solving public problems. In that environment, it is worth revisiting an old democratic idea with new relevance: sortition, or the selection of public decision-makers by lottery from the citizenry.

The United States should incorporate sortition into its governing institutions, especially in legislative and deliberative bodies, because it can reduce the influence of money, weaken destructive partisanship, and give ordinary citizens a more direct and meaningful role in self-government. Sortition is not a magical cure for every political problem, and it should not simply replace all elections overnight. But as a democratic tool, it offers a powerful corrective to many of the failures of the current system.

Elections have serious structural weaknesses

Americans often treat elections as the only democratic method that matters, but elections have clear limitations. Running for office requires money, connections, name recognition, media skill, and a willingness to campaign constantly. Those requirements narrow the field long before any voter casts a ballot. In practice, electoral politics tends to favor the wealthy, the well-connected, the highly ambitious, and the politically professional. This does not mean all elected officials are bad people. It means the system itself filters out many ordinary citizens who may have sound judgment, practical knowledge, and a strong sense of civic duty but no interest in becoming career politicians.

Elections also create incentives that distort public service. Candidates must appeal to donors, activists, party leaders, and media audiences. Once in office, they must think about the next campaign. That pressure encourages short-term messaging over long-term problem-solving. It rewards confrontation, performance, and partisan signaling. In many cases, officials are not merely trying to govern well; they are trying to survive politically in an environment built around perpetual competition.

Sortition addresses these weaknesses by changing who gets selected and what incentives they face. A randomly selected citizen does not need to raise money, flatter donors, or spend years building a political brand. That alone would remove one of the most corrupting pressures in public life: the need to secure office through expensive campaigns.

Sortition can reduce corruption by weakening the role of money and careerism

One of the strongest arguments for sortition is that it can reduce some major forms of political corruption. In an electoral system, organized wealth has many points of entry: campaign contributions, lobbying, advertising, independent expenditures, and the revolving door between office and private influence. Even when these practices are legal, they create a system in which access and attention are unequally distributed.

Random selection would not eliminate corruption in the absolute sense. Any institution can be influenced or manipulated if it is poorly designed. But sortition can reduce the most familiar and damaging forms of electoral corruption because randomly selected citizens would not owe their position to donors, party machines, or campaign consultants. They would not have spent years making promises to interest groups in order to win office. They would not need to constantly calculate how each vote affects their reelection chances. Their legitimacy would come from equal citizenship, not campaign success.

That change matters. It shifts public office away from career advancement and toward civic service. If service in a legislative chamber were like jury duty—serious, temporary, compensated, and supported by staff and expert testimony—public decision-making would become less about ambition and more about responsibility. Citizens chosen by lot would have less reason to treat office as a platform for self-promotion and more reason to focus on the merits of the issues before them.

Sortition can reduce partisanship by changing how people deliberate

Modern American politics is intensely partisan in part because elections reward partisan behavior. Candidates need primary voters, activist energy, and party infrastructure. They are pushed to define themselves against the other side. Once in office, they often continue acting as party representatives rather than independent public servants. The result is a political culture in which compromise looks like betrayal and outrage becomes a political resource.

Sortition offers a different model. A randomly selected body would be descriptively representative of the public: different ages, regions, occupations, educational backgrounds, races, religions, and political opinions. Such a body would still contain disagreement, but it would not be organized primarily around partisan competition for power. It would begin not with campaign slogans, but with a shared civic task.

Evidence from citizens’ assemblies and deliberative mini-publics in various countries suggests that ordinary people, when given time, balanced information, and structured deliberation, often become more thoughtful and less tribal than professional politicians. They listen. They revise their views. They distinguish between talking points and practical consequences. They are not free from bias, but they are often less trapped by party incentives.

That difference is crucial. Sortition does not assume that citizens are perfect. It assumes that democracy works better when public judgment is formed through deliberation rather than constant campaigning. By replacing some partisan competition with structured citizen deliberation, the country could reduce polarization and restore some measure of political trust.

Sortition empowers ordinary people in a way elections often do not

Defenders of the current system often say elections empower the people because everyone gets a vote. But voting every few years is a thin form of participation. For most citizens, political influence begins and ends at the ballot box. In between elections, they become spectators to a professional political class.

Sortition offers a fuller democratic ideal: not just the right to choose rulers, but the possibility of ruling and being ruled in turn. That principle goes back to ancient democratic thought. A free society should not reserve public office for a narrow political elite. It should treat citizenship itself as a qualification for meaningful public responsibility.

Random selection expresses a powerful democratic truth: ordinary people are capable of governing. Teachers, mechanics, nurses, office workers, parents, retirees, and students all possess forms of knowledge that professional politicians often lack. They know how policies affect daily life. They understand their communities. They are not all policy experts, but expertise can be provided through hearings, staff support, and access to competing viewpoints. What matters most in many political decisions is not technical mastery alone, but judgment, fairness, and a willingness to weigh tradeoffs in good faith.

A system that includes sortition would send a message that democracy is not a performance put on by political specialists. It is a shared civic enterprise. That message could strengthen public legitimacy because citizens are more likely to trust institutions that visibly include people like themselves.

Sortition should be designed carefully, not romanticized

A persuasive case for sortition must be serious about institutional design. Random selection should not mean random chaos. If sortition were used, selected citizens would need training, professional staff, independent ethics rules, transparent procedures, and enough time to learn. Service should be compensated so that participation is realistic for working people, caregivers, and citizens of modest means. Selection methods should ensure broad representativeness and allow limited exemptions for hardship, while preventing the system from becoming skewed toward only those who can afford to serve.

There are also roles where elections may still be appropriate. Executive leadership in particular raises questions about speed, accountability, and national coordination. Rather than abolishing elections entirely, the stronger case is for integrating sortition where it can improve democratic legitimacy and decision quality: second chambers, citizens’ assemblies, redistricting bodies, ethics commissions, constitutional review panels, and portions of legislatures. Over time, if those institutions prove effective, their role could expand.

This mixed approach is more persuasive than a total replacement model because it recognizes that democracy can use more than one mechanism. Elections provide public choice and broad accountability. Sortition provides representation without campaign distortion. Used together, they could balance each other’s weaknesses.

The core democratic question is who gets to govern

At bottom, the argument for sortition is moral as much as institutional. A democracy should not quietly drift into rule by the ambitious, the affluent, and the professionally political while calling that arrangement popular self-government. If political power is consistently filtered through money, branding, and partisan machinery, then the people are not truly governing. They are merely choosing among elites shaped by forces they do not control.

Sortition challenges that arrangement. It insists that public office should not be treated as a prize won in a permanent contest, but as a civic responsibility distributed among equals. It broadens the meaning of representation from “someone speaks for you” to “people like you actually take part in governing.” That is a more demanding and more democratic vision.

Conclusion

The United States should adopt sortition as a significant part of its democratic system because it can reduce the influence of money, soften partisan conflict, and empower ordinary citizens to participate directly in public decision-making. The Case for Sortition: A Democratic Revolution Beyond Elections

Introduction

The United States is a nation built on the principle of self-governance, yet its political system remains deeply flawed by corruption, partisan gridlock, and the undemocratic influence of wealth and power. Traditional elections—where candidates are selected by wealthy donors, corporate interests, and partisan machinery—have become a farce, prioritizing campaign finance over public representation. The solution lies not in reforming elections but in replacing them entirely with sortition, a system of random citizen selection for legislative and executive leadership.

Sortition, derived from the Greek sortire ("to draw lots"), has been the foundation of democracy in ancient Athens, Sparta, and other classical societies. It ensures that political power is not concentrated in the hands of a few wealthy elites but is distributed among ordinary citizens, free from the corrupting influence of money and partisan bias. By adopting sortition, the United States could eliminate political corruption, reduce extreme partisanship, and restore genuine democratic participation—empowering the people, not the powerful.

I. Sortition Eliminates Political Corruption

A. The Corrupting Influence of Money in Elections

No system is more corrupt than one where elections are bought and sold by wealthy donors. The U.S. Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United decision opened the floodgates for corporate and dark-money influence, allowing billionaires and lobbyists to dictate policy through campaign contributions. The average congressional candidate now receives $1.2 million in donations, while the average voter spends just $30 on elections. This disparity ensures that the richest 1% control the political process, while ordinary citizens have no meaningful voice.

Sortition removes this financial barrier entirely. Since leadership is selected randomly from a pool of qualified citizens, there is no need for expensive campaigns, no need for corporate donations, and no need for wealthy candidates to buy influence. The system is democratically neutral—no one can buy their way into power, and no one can be bribed out of it.

B. The End of Lobbying and Special Interests

Lobbyists and corporate lobbyists spend billions to sway legislation, often through undisclosed donations, campaign contributions, and backroom deals. Sortition would eliminate this entirely because elected officials would no longer be beholden to donors. Instead, they would represent the general will of the people, not the interests of the wealthy.

In ancient Athens, the Boule (a council of randomly selected citizens) was immune to corruption because it was not elected. The same principle applies today. A system where leaders are chosen by lot ensures that no single industry or billionaire can dominate policy-making.

C. The Transparency of a Random System

Elections are shrouded in secrecy—campaign finance reports are often incomplete, and dark money flows undetected. Sortition, however, is fully transparent. Since leadership is selected through a public, unbiased process, there is no possibility of hidden influence. Every citizen has an equal chance of being selected, and the system is open to scrutiny.

In contrast, today’s political system is a black box where money, media, and partisanship dictate outcomes. Sortition would bring accountability—because no one can buy their way into power, and no one can be bribed out of it.

II. Sortition Reduces Partisanship and Restores Unity

A. The Problem of Polarized Partisanship

American politics has become a two-party war, where each side demonizes the other, refuses to compromise, and prioritizes ideological purity over governance. The result is gridlock, where bills are filibustered, laws are blocked, and the public suffers under stagnant policy.

Partisanship is not inevitable—it is created by the electoral system. When leaders are chosen by a small, wealthy elite, they feel no obligation to work across party lines. Sortition, however, would break this cycle because:

  • No single party can dominate—since leadership is selected randomly, no one group can monopolize power.
  • Compromise becomes necessary—if leaders are not beholden to a single party, they must seek common ground.
  • The public’s will is the priority—since the system is not partisan, leaders must represent the majority, not their base.

B. The Ancient Athenian Model: A System of Shared Leadership

In ancient Athens, the Ekklesia (Assembly) was not a single-party body but a citizen-led democracy. While the Assembly was dominated by wealthy landowners, the Boule (Council of 500) was selected by lot, ensuring that even the poorest citizens had a voice.

This system worked because:

  • No single faction could dominate—the Council was balanced, and debates were open to all.
  • Decisions were made collectively—rather than through partisan votes, leaders were selected to facilitate discussion.
  • The people felt represented—since leadership was not concentrated in a few, there was no sense of exclusion.

Today, we could adapt this model by:

  • Randomly selecting a mixed council (legislators and executives) from a pool of qualified citizens.
  • Allowing for deliberative assemblies where leaders must justify their positions to the public.
  • Ensuring that no single party can block progress—since leadership is not partisan, compromise becomes the default.

C. The End of "Winner-Takes-All" Politics

Today, elections are won by the candidate who spends the most money, not the one who best represents the people. Sortition would eliminate this outcome because:

  • No candidate can buy votes—since leadership is selected randomly, no one can manipulate elections.
  • The system favors quality over quantity—since all citizens have an equal chance, the best ideas—not the most expensive ads—will prevail.
  • Parties lose their monopoly on power—since leadership is not elected, no single party can claim exclusive authority.

This would restore democracy to its true purpose: a system where the people, not the wealthy, decide who leads.

III. Sortition Empowers Ordinary People

A. The Illusion of Democracy in Elections

Elections are often called "democratic," but they are not. They allow a small percentage of the population to vote, while the rest are excluded from meaningful participation. The average voter has no real influence—campaigns are dominated by elites, and policy is shaped by lobbyists, not the public.

Sortition changes this by:

  • Giving every citizen a voice—since leadership is selected randomly, even those who don’t vote have a say.
  • Ensuring that power is distributed—no longer is leadership concentrated in a few, but spread across the population.
  • Creating a system of shared responsibility—since leadership is not elected, citizens must engage in deliberation, not just passive voting.

B. The Power of Deliberative Democracy

Sortition is not just about selecting leaders—it is about building a more participatory democracy. In ancient Athens, citizens were expected to engage in debate, to question leaders, and to hold them accountable. Today, we have deliberative polling and citizen assemblies, but they are rare and often ignored.

A full sortition system would:

  • Require leaders to justify their decisions—since they are not elected, they must explain themselves to the public.
  • Encourage civic engagement—citizens would have a stake in the political process, not just a passive role.
  • Reduce the "tyranny of the majority"—since leadership is not elected, no single group can dominate, ensuring fair representation.

C. The Case for a "Randomized Republic"

The philosopher Michael Sandel argues that democracy requires deliberation, not just elections. Sortition would create a system where:

  • Leaders are not beholden to donors or parties—they must serve the public interest.
  • The public can challenge decisions—since leadership is not elected, citizens can hold leaders accountable.
  • The system is resilient to manipulation—no one can buy influence, and no one can be bribed out of power.

This is not just a reform—it is a revolution in how we think about democracy.

IV. The Practicality of Sortition in the United States

A. How It Could Be Implemented

Sortition is not an impossible dream—it is a testable model. Countries like:

  • Iceland (which uses a citizen assembly for policy deliberation)
  • Switzerland (which has direct democracy elements)
  • The Netherlands (which uses randomized councils in some local governments)

have shown that sortition is feasible. The U.S. could adopt a hybrid system:

  1. Randomly select a mixed council (legislators and executives) from a pool of qualified citizens.
  2. Use deliberative assemblies where leaders must justify their positions.
  3. Allow for public input—citizens can propose laws and debate them in open forums.
  4. Gradually expand the system—starting with local governments, then state legislatures, and finally the federal level.

B. The Benefits of a Gradual Transition

A full sortition system would not be implemented overnight. Instead, we could:

  • Start with local governments—where corruption and partisanship are most visible.
  • Use sortition for key policy decisions—such as budget approvals or major legislation.
  • Phase out partisan elections over time, replacing them with random selection.

This approach would:

  • Reduce corruption incrementally—as more leaders are selected randomly, the influence of money decreases.
  • Build public trust—as citizens see the benefits of sortition, they will demand its expansion.
  • Avoid sudden shocks—a full transition would be smoother than a sudden overhaul.

C. The Resistance to Change

Some will argue that sortition is un-American or too radical. But democracy has always been a process of evolution, not a static system. The Founding Fathers themselves were skeptical of pure democracy, preferring a mixed constitution—and sortition is a natural extension of that principle.

In an era defined by disillusionment with politics, the United States clings to a ritual that is increasingly failing its promises: elections. Against this backdrop, an old democratic technology has re-emerged as a radical, yet deeply principled alternative: sortition—the selection of public officials by lottery from the citizenry. Far from a utopian fantasy, sortition has a strong historical pedigree, a growing body of empirical support from modern deliberative assemblies, and a powerful ethical core: political power should be a temporary public duty broadly shared, not a career captured by the few.

A comprehensive shift toward sortition-based governance for legislative and executive leadership would represent a profound re-founding of American democracy. While it raises serious design questions, its advantages are far-reaching. It attacks systemic corruption at its roots, defuses destructive partisanship, and elevates ordinary citizens from passive spectators to active stewards of their own political community.

  1. Breaking the structural link between money and power

The defining pathology of contemporary elections is not simply that some donors are influential; it is that the electoral mechanism intrinsically rewards dependence on money, marketing, and manipulation.

  • Candidates must raise enormous sums to compete.
  • Parties and outside groups use targeted advertising, data analytics, and fear-based messaging.
  • Lobbyists and major donors gain privileged access because elected officials know they will soon need more contributions.

Even the most idealistic politician is locked inside a system that constantly pressures them to court financial support and media exposure. This is not a collection of individual moral failings; it is an incentive structure.

Sortition detonates that structure.

If legislative and executive leaders are chosen at random from a broad, eligible pool of citizens:

  • There are no campaigns to fund.
  • There are no donors to please.
  • There is no need to shape policy around optics for the next election.
  • There is no permanent political class building brand and power.

Interest groups could still advocate, provide information, and attempt persuasion, but they would no longer be investing in a stable set of career decision-makers who need money to survive politically. Influence becomes more diffuse, less predictable, and easier to check through transparency and rotation.

To strengthen this:

  • Terms would be strictly limited and non-renewable.
  • Lobbying contacts would be fully logged and publicly accessible.
  • Conflict-of-interest rules would be strict, with meaningful penalties.

By design, sortition decouples public office from the wealth engines that now distort representation. It addresses corruption not by chasing bad actors, but by making the most common corrupt pathways structurally unworkable.

Modern elections reward those who can mobilize anger, fear, and loyalty to party identity. In safe districts, the real contest is often the primary, pushing candidates toward ideological extremes. Social media amplification, partisan media ecosystems, and professional campaign messaging further radicalize and oversimplify.

Sortition offers a different logic.

A randomly selected legislature would resemble the country in its actual distribution of views, identities, and life experiences. It would likely include:

  • Conservatives, liberals, moderates, independents, the disengaged, and the disillusioned.
  • People from varied classes, races, ages, geographies, and professions.
  • People who have never seen politics as a personal brand or team sport.

Because these citizens are:

  • Not running for re-election.
  • Not beholden to a party machine for their political survival.
  • Not trying to maintain a public persona for donors or media.

They have weaker incentives to posture and stronger incentives to deliberate. We already see this in:

  • Citizens’ assemblies in Ireland (on abortion, marriage equality, constitutional questions).
  • Deliberative polls and citizens’ juries across Europe, Canada, and some U.S. localities.

Ordinary people, given time, balanced information, and responsibility, consistently show they are capable of nuance, compromise, and empathy that far outperforms the behavior incentivized in electoral politics.

In a sortition system:

  • Party labels may still exist as ideological reference points, but their power to gatekeep office collapses.
  • Media incentives shift from horse-race coverage to scrutiny of processes, evidence, and outcomes.
  • Decision-making bodies become more like large, standing citizen juries than campaign arenas.

The public sees itself—literally, statistically—in its institutions. That alone can lower the “us vs. them” temperature that elections constantly inflame.

Elections promise political equality—one person, one vote—but deliver political inequality—some people, many donations, outsized influence; most people, episodic, low-impact participation.

Sortition is a direct assertion that:

  • Every competent adult citizen is not just equal in theory, but eligible in fact to govern.
  • Government is a civic service distributed broadly, not a specialized career preserved for a narrow professional-political class.

a) Descriptive representation by default

Random selection, if done from a genuinely inclusive pool, naturally mirrors the population:

  • Women, minorities, working-class citizens, people outside coastal metros, renters, caregivers—groups chronically underrepresented in elected bodies—enter power in proportion to their presence in society.

Serving becomes a high-intensity civic education experience:

  • Selected citizens receive training in lawmaking, ethics, critical thinking, and policy analysis.
  • They are supported by non-partisan expert staff and open hearings.
  • After their limited term, they return to their communities with deep institutional understanding.

c) Equalizing voice and access

When “people like you” are literally in office by design, engagement stops feeling futile.

  • Public input is not funneled solely through intermediaries loyal to donors and parties.
  • Town halls, hearings, and consultations connect citizens with other citizens entrusted to decide, lowering psychological barriers to participation and trust.

The effect is subtle but profound: democracy shifts from “watching them” to “taking turns doing it.”

  1. Institutional design: how a sortition system could work

Our current electoral system has become democracy's greatest enemy. Politicians spend more time fundraising than governing, with members of Congress dedicating 30-70% of their time to soliciting donations. This creates an obvious conflict of interest: lawmakers become beholden to their funders rather than their constituents. We end up selecting for charisma and wealth rather than wisdom and competence.

Under sortition, these corrupting influences disappear overnight. Randomly selected citizens owe their positions to no one. They cannot be bought because they never asked to be chosen. They have no electoral promises to keep except their oath to serve the public good.

Breaking the Stranglehold of Partisanship

Perhaps nowhere is electoral dysfunction more apparent than in America's toxic partisan divide. Politicians must appeal to increasingly extreme primary voters and partisan donors, pushing them toward ideological extremes. The result is a system where compromise becomes betrayal and governing becomes impossible.

Sortition bypasses this entirely. Random selection would produce legislatures that reflect the true diversity of American opinion rather than the polarized extremes that dominate primaries. Citizens chosen by lottery arrive without partisan baggage or ideological litmus tests. They can evaluate issues on their merits rather than through partisan filters.

Ireland's Citizens' Assembly demonstrates this potential. Their recommendations, later approved by referendum, showed how ordinary people can tackle controversial issues when freed from partisan constraints.

American legislatures bear little resemblance to the people they claim to represent. Congress is overwhelmingly male, white, wealthy, and college-educated. The average House member is worth over $1 million while the typical American family has $121,000 in net worth. This isn't representation—it's oligarchy with democratic window dressing.

Sortition would create genuinely representative bodies for the first time in American history. Random selection naturally produces demographic diversity that no electoral system can match. Working parents, teachers, farmers, and factory workers would sit alongside lawyers and business owners. Young and old, rich and poor, urban and rural Americans would share power in proportion to their actual numbers.

This isn't just about fairness—it's about better outcomes. Research consistently shows that diverse groups make better decisions than homogeneous ones. A legislature of randomly selected citizens would bring a breadth of life experience and perspective that career politicians simply cannot match.

Elections create the illusion of citizen control while actually concentrating power in the hands of political elites. Voters get to choose between pre-selected candidates who share similar backgrounds and are beholden to similar interests. It's democracy's equivalent of being offered chocolate or vanilla ice cream when what you really want is pizza.

American democracy faces an existential crisis. Trust in institutions approaches historic lows while polarization reaches dangerous heights. Traditional reforms—campaign finance limits, redistricting reform, term limits—address symptoms while leaving the underlying disease untreated.

Only sortition attacks the root causes of democratic dysfunction. By eliminating electoral incentives, it removes corruption at its source. By bypassing partisan primaries, it enables genuine deliberation. By empowering ordinary citizens, it restores democracy's promise.

The ancient Athenians understood that democracy means rule by ordinary citizens, not professional politicians. It's time for America to rediscover this wisdom. Elections have become auctions for influence. Campaigns in the U.S. now cost billions of dollars, with the 2020 federal elections alone exceeding $14 billion. The majority of this funding comes from a vanishingly small fraction of the population—0.01% of Americans contribute nearly 40% of all political donations. By randomly selecting citizens to serve in office—with term limits, intensive public training, and full transparency—there is no incentive to curry favor with donors. A randomly chosen citizen legislator has neither the ambition to run for re-election nor the connections to lobbyists. They are not beholden to PACs or superdelegates. They serve their fellow citizens out of civic duty, not self-interest. In this system, corruption cannot take root because it cannot be bought.

Ending Partisanship: From Tribal Warfare to Deliberative Governance

The second crisis of American democracy is partisan extremism. Politicians are incentivized to appeal to the fringes of their base—because primary elections, gerrymandered districts, and partisan media reward polarization. Moderates are punished; ideologues are rewarded. Sortition breaks this cycle. Randomly selected citizens come from all walks of life—teachers, nurses, mechanics, farmers, retirees, single parents, immigrants. They do not belong to a party. They do not have ideological brands to protect. They are not trained in media spectacle. When brought together in diverse, demographically representative panels and equipped with expert briefings, deliberative forums, and facilitation by nonpartisan professionals, they consistently produce more moderate, consensus-driven outcomes than elected bodies.

Decades of deliberative polling experiments—from Oregon’s Citizen Initiative Review to the French Citizen Convention on Climate—demonstrate that ordinary people, when given time, information, and structured dialogue, make wiser, more equitable decisions than politicians under electoral pressure. In France’s 2020–2021 Climate Convention, randomly selected citizens proposed 149 measures to reduce emissions; 146 were adopted by Parliament without amendment. Sortition is not the end of democracy—it is its redemption.

Sortition. Random selection. The same method the ancient Athenians used to choose jurors, magistrates, and even generals—not because they were naive, but because they understood something we have forgotten: Power corrupts. Elections entrench it. But randomness? Randomness liberates.

Imagine this:

Instead of billionaires funding Super PACs to elect Congresspeople who owe them favors—we randomly select 435 citizens, just like jury duty, but for governance. Not because they’re “the best,” but because they’re representative. A teacher from Ohio. A veteran from Tennessee. A nurse from Florida. A single dad from Detroit. A teenager who just turned 18—yes, 18!—we select them all, proportionally, to reflect the true face of America: racial, economic, geographic, educational.

These citizens would be compensated fairly, trained intensively in policy, ethics, and civic deliberation, and given the full power of legislation and executive decision-making—for one term only. No re-elections. No campaign cash. No lobbyists whispering in ears. Just us.

Us.

Not the special interest-indoctrinated. Not the Ivy League-turned-power-brokers. Not the carbon-copy politicians who graduated from the same donor-family feeder schools.

Us.

And here’s the magic: When you can’t run for office again, you have no reason to betray the people. When your time is finite, your loyalty is fixed—to your neighbors, your community, your conscience.

Corruption? Eliminated. Because you can’t sell influence if you’re gone in 18 months.
Partisanship? Weakened. Because your group isn’t your party—it’s your block, your neighborhood, your child’s school.
Accountability? Stronger than ever. Because every decision is made in full public view, with real citizen oversight, not behind closed doors in the Capitol’s backrooms.

And what of expertise? Don’t we need “professionals”? Let me be clear: A doctor doesn’t fix your heart because they won an election. They fix it because they trained. So why do we think governance should be run by people who won a popularity contest? We hire experts to design bridges, to treat illness, to fly planes. Why not to craft public policy?

We don’t need career politicians.

We need citizen legislators.

We need ordinary people—not trained in politics, but trained in humanity.

And what about those who say, “Random people can’t govern”? Then teach them. That’s our responsibility. Give them time. Give them resources. Give them dignity. We sent citizens into a courtroom to decide life and death in a trial—they can decide healthcare reform, climate policy, or education funding. If we trust them with the fate of a stranger accused of murder… why don’t we trust them with the fate of our country?

This isn’t utopian fantasy.

It’s ancient wisdom revived.

It’s the French Revolution’s call for “citizen sovereignty” reborn.

It’s the Canadian Citizens’ Assembly on Electoral Reform—where randomly selected citizens, after months of deliberation, recommended overwhelming change… and were dismissed by the politicians who feared losing power.

Look at us now.

The almighty ballot box has failed us.

It didn’t stop the Iraq War.

It didn’t prevent Wall Street’s 2008 heist.

It didn’t halt the climate collapse.

It didn’t end machine politics, gerrymandering, voter suppression, or the descent of our public dialogue into rage-fueled digital theater.

But sortition—sortition can save us.

It can restore the sacred covenant between the people and their government.

It can turn the Capitol into a reflection of Main Street.

It can say to every child who grows up poor, black, brown, queer, disabled, or just plain tired of being ignored: Your voice doesn’t need a campaign coach to be heard. You don’t need to be charismatic, wealthy, or connected. Just you. Just your truth. That’s enough.

We are not too stupid to govern.

We are too trained to believe we can’t.

Let’s stop pretending that flipping a switch in a voting booth makes us free.

True freedom? True democracy?

Is when ordinary people, chosen by chance, hold the levers of power—not as guests, but as sovereigns.

I am not asking you to vote for this.

I am asking you to become this.

Let us scorn the cult of the candidate.

Let us rend the paper ballots that only pretend to empower.

Let us build a new Congress—not of politicians, but of parents, plumbers, pastors, and private citizens.

Let us select our leaders by lottery.

And watch as the country trembles with the awe of true, uncorrupted, unmediated democracy.

Let us abolish elections.

Let us empower the people.

Let us choose by chance… and govern with conscience.

The people are ready.

Are you?

Thank you.
